articles.title: Gov. Healey takes emergency action to block effort to suspend abortion law
articles.text:
Gov. Healey takes emergency action to block effort to suspend abortion law | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey turns to the women gathered behind her after signing an abortion bill at the State House on Aug. 10. (Jessica Rinaldi/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)
Gov. Maura Healey signed an emergency preamble Friday to force a law removing barriers to abortions later in pregnancy to take effect immediately, a move that blocks efforts to suspend the statute while its opponents move a repeal question toward the 2028 ballot.
The emergency preamble, filed with the Secretary of State William Galvin's office on Friday afternoon, prevents the law from any suspension attempts over the next two years, a spokesperson for the governor's office confirmed. The law was set to take effect on Sunday, Nov. 9, according to the House clerk's office.
Healey wrote that "any further delay in implementing the Act would prolong uncertainty for patients, families, physicians and health care institutions, and risk further harm to the health and safety of women in Massachusetts."
Galvin's office is processing petitions from a group seeking to put a repeal referendum before voters in 2028.
Sam Miele, chair of the Compassionate Care Coalition, led by the Massachusetts Citizens for Life and Massachusetts Family Action, said the group dropped off 113,477 signatures certified by local clerks with Galvin's office on Friday. That surpasses the 37,289 signatures needed to make the 2028 ballot and 49,719 signatures to suspend the law in the interim.
The law, which is based on bills that raced through the Legislature before the end of scheduled formal sessions in July, removes four criteria from the statute that allowed abortions at or beyond 24 weeks in life-threatening situations for the patient or fetus. Instead, the law defers to providers' medical judgement for whether to perform an abortion.
In an Substack post Friday afternoon elaborating on her decision to take emergency action, Healey said "at least nine patients" have been denied abortion care in Massachusetts since the law was signed in August and said that "two more years of women being denied care" is "not a reality I can accept."
"The repeal campaign can continue its work, and Massachusetts voters will have their say," she wrote. "If they choose to repeal the law, we will respect their decision. But families should not have to go without the care they need while that process plays out."
"Since the Prioritizing Patient Access to Care Act was signed into law in August, at least nine Massachusetts patients facing devastating pregnancy complications have been denied compassionate abortion care here in the Commonwealth while waiting for the law to take effect. Today, Governor Healey took decisive action to address this public health emergency, removing unnecessary delays and ensuring patients can access the care they need when they need it,” said Kathleen Melendy, Reproductive Equity Now’s Massachusetts State Director.
Said Miele: "The prior abortion law in Massachusetts allowed abortions after 24 weeks if the mother's life was in danger. The only thing this new law does is allow babies who pose no threat to the life of the mother to be killed at will in the womb at nine months. Governor Healey, you must explain to the voters why that is an emergency."
Dr. Rebecca Brendel, president of the Massachusetts Medical Society, applauded the governor's decision.
"The MMS remains firmly committed to protecting clinical autonomy and access to comprehensive, equitable reproductive health care," Brendel said in a statement. "Physicians bear the responsibility to make complex, individualized clinical treatment recommendations based on scientific evidence, established standards of care, and circumstances unique to our patients. Decisions regarding abortion care later in pregnancy should be no different."

articles.title: Signing expanded abortion law, Gov. Healey cites stories of 'anguish and heartache'
articles.text:
Signing expanded abortion law, Gov. Healey cites stories of 'anguish and heartache' | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Gov. Maura Healey signs a bill about abortion access in Massachusetts at the State House on Aug. 10, 2026. (Jessica Rinaldi/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)
After lawmakers fast-tracked the bill, Gov. Maura Healey on Monday signed legislation on Monday that removes restrictions on abortions after 24 weeks of gestation, a change that supporters say will help more patients stay in-state to receive care.
The law (H 5595) eliminates the existing four-pronged framework enabling abortions for pregnancies at or beyond 24 weeks in life-threatening situations for the patient or fetus, instead writing a new law that states "an abortion may be performed by a physician based upon the professional judgment of the physician."
"We've heard so many stories — stories that are filled with a lot of pain and anguish and heartache and a lot of trauma. We heard stories about the worst moments of a person's life, of a couple's life," Healey said, surrounded by lawmakers, advocates and physicians at a press conference she hosted in her ceremonial office. "We're signing this law today so that new patients, people we won't know or won't meet, will be able to get the care that they need in Massachusetts."
The bill was filed at the start of the two-year session by Rep. Christine Barber, who is running this fall for an open Senate seat. It began to take off on July 22 when it was released from the House Ways and Means Committee and was pushed through both branches in a flurry of late-July legislating. The new law will go into effect in 90 days, Healey's office confirmed.
"We know that protecting abortion access and reproductive health care has been under fire," Healey said, noting the U.S. Supreme Court's decision to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022 and adding, "Today, one in three women in America live in a state with an abortion ban."
The House on July 22  voted 119-33 to pass the bill, with all Republicans who voted casting their votes against it. Democrats who rejected the bill included Reps. Brian Ashe, Lisa Field, Michael Finn, Dennis Gallagher, Russell Holmes, Christopher Markey, Francisco Paulino, Alan Silvia and Jeffrey Turco. Rep. Susannah Whipps, the chamber's only Independent member, voted yes.
The Senate on July 31 passed the bill with a 15-4 standing vote.
According to Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Mike Day, it's the fourth time in 16 years that lawmakers revisited the issue "in an effort to get it right, to get government out of the way of a health issue, and to lessen the trauma inflicted on pregnant women, who are suddenly confronted with unbelievably tragic news about their pregnancies more than six months into their term."
"We hear that some medical professionals are still uncomfortable with the specific language restrictions that they say continues to interfere with their professional medical judgment, and that some patients continue to have to leave the commonwealth or stay and endure unnecessary trauma because a treating physician is afraid that they will somehow run afoul of the law based on those restrictions," Day, who was at the bill signing Monday, said on the House floor before the late July vote.
Kate Dineen and her husband Alex Lawton recalled the journey they took to Washington, D.C. in 2021, when Dineen was 33 weeks pregnant and learned her baby had suffered a stroke in utero.
"He would either die or survive for some period of time with a spectrum of devastating outcomes. And so upon learning of the prognosis, I asked, 'What are my options?' And I will never forget the response. 'You may still be able to explore termination if you're able to travel,'" Dineen said. "Travel where? We were standing in our kitchen in Boston, just less than a mile from some of the best hospitals in the country."
The diagnosis didn't qualify for an exception, Dineen said, and their doctor's "highly capable hands were tied by Massachusetts state law."
The Massachusetts Health and Hospital Association, Beth Israel Lahey Health, Mass General Brigham, Tufts Medicine and UMass Memorial Health in mid-July sent a letter of support to House Speaker Ron Mariano, writing that the state's existing statutory framework "does not adequately meet the needs of all patients."
According to Department of Public Health Data, there were 99 abortions done at 24 weeks or later in 2024, compared to 84 in 2023. There was a sharp increase in the total number of abortions in Massachusetts in 2024 compared to those done in 2023, which public health officials have said was due to out-of-state patients accessing care through telehealth.
"The reality is that medicine does not always fit into clearly defined legal categories," Worcester Sen. Robyn Kennedy said on the Senate floor on July 31. "Physicians need the ability to use their medical judgment and advise their patients when facing complex and rapidly changing medical circumstances."
Public Health Committee Chair Rep. Marjorie Decker said last month that the legislation "does not tell a patient what decision to make. It does not force anyone to have an abortion. It does not take decision-making away from the patients."
The Massachusetts Family Institute on Aug. 3 urged people, "Tell the governor to veto radical late-term abortion!" The institute called the bill "a dangerous attempt to remove virtually all remaining protections in the Commonwealth for unborn babies."
Massachusetts Family Action sent out an email on Aug. 7, writing that the Legislature "passed one of the most extreme abortion bills in the country — allowing abortion at any point in pregnancy, for any reason, outside the safeguards of a hospital." The group plans a webinar Tuesday on "what's really in this bill — and how you can help elect leaders who will protect life."

articles.title: Activists launch effort to suspend Massachusetts' new abortion law — and put it on the 2028 ballot
articles.text:
Activists launch effort to suspend Massachusetts' new abortion law — and put it on the 2028 ballot | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey turns to the women gathered behind her after signing an abortion bill at the State House on Aug. 10. (Jessica Rinaldi/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's daily morning newsletter, WBUR Today. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here.
It's Friday. Before you log off for Labor Day weekend, let's cut through this morning's dense fog and get to some breaking news:
Another ballot campaign enters: While voters in Massachusetts were casting their ballots in Tuesday's primary, some local activists were quietly making moves for the 2028 election. Secretary of State Bill Galvin's office confirmed yesterday to WBUR that a referendum petition was filed Tuesday on the abortion rights law signed by Gov. Maura Healey last month. The filing marks the start of an effort this fall to potentially pause the new law and put a question on the ballot in 2028 that would ask voters to repeal it.
What does the law do? The law — which was signed by Healey on Aug. 10 after zooming through the State House — removes restrictions on abortions after 24 weeks of gestation, leaving the decision up to "the professional judgment of the physician." It's set to take effect on Nov. 8.
What was the reason for it? Supporters cited stories of "pain and anguish" from residents due to the previous rules for abortions after 24 weeks, which only allowed the procedure in specific circumstances, such life-threatening situations for the patient or fetus. "These situations are incredibly rare, and the decisions should be made between patients, their families, and their doctor — not by politicians and the government," Healey told WBUR in a statement Thursday.
Who's behind the repeal effort? The referendum effort is being led by two local anti-abortion groups: Massachusetts Citizens for Life and Massachusetts Family Action, a 501(c)(4) group affiliated with the Massachusetts Family Institute. "We have not pursued a referendum after every abortion law passed in Massachusetts, but this law crosses a fundamentally different line," Myrna Maloney Flynn, the president of Mass Citizens for Life, told WBUR. Flynn objected to the law's removal of viability limits and said it allows hospitals to send patients to Planned Parenthood clinics for "complex, dangerous late-term abortions rather than providing that care within better-equipped hospital facilities."
What's next? Referendums work a little differently than the usual biennial ballot question process in Massachusetts. According to Galvin's office, supporters have to collect at least 37,289 signatures this fall to get a question on the 2028 ballot asking voters to repeal or uphold the law. And if they get over 49,719 signatures, they can actually suspend the law from taking effect until that 2028 vote. (Sam Miele, the director of Massachusetts Family Action, said in an email their goal is to suspend the law.) Those signatures are due to local clerks by Oct. 23 and to Galvin's office by Nov. 6.
Watch this space: Healey can block the possibility of the new law getting suspended if she adds an "emergency preamble" to its language. Healey's office declined to say if they're considering that option Thursday, but she's done so before — with the 2024 gun law that's subject to a referendum this fall.
On the street: Boston Mayor Michelle Wu's administration and the MBTA just dropped an updated design this morning for the Blue Hill Avenue project. WBUR's Andrea Perdomo-Hernandez reports the new plan comes after concerns about the $160 million transformation of the corridor from residents and some local elected officials.
What's different? Andrea reports the new design keeps the center-running bus lane, but adds 42 more parking spaces and keeps two car lanes through most of the project area. Meanwhile, previous plans for bike lanes on both sides of the street are being scaled back and replaced with a two-way sidewalk-level bike path on one side. Scroll through the renderings here.
Not bluffing: More than 1,300 unionized workers at the Encore Boston Harbor casino are set to go on strike this morning. The Everett resort casino's housekeepers, cooks, bartenders and slot attendants want the same wage standards as other hotel workers in the Boston area, plus bigger company contributions to their healthcare plan. But negotiations remain an impasse after months of bargaining. (Encore says it remains open and operational during the strike.)
Every vote counts: Longtime state Sen. Will Brownsberger is moving to request a full recount, after the initial results from Tuesday's primary show him losing to Wu-backed challenger Dan Lander by just three votes. WBUR's Gin Dumcius reports that Brownsberger's campaign expects the recount to happen next week. The deadline to formally request it is today at 5 p.m.
P.S. — What technology does the Trump administration plan to buy from a Massachusetts company for immigration enforcement? Take our Boston News Quiz and test your knowledge of this week's stories.

articles.title: 2028 referendum supporters say they have enough signatures to suspend new Mass. abortion law. Now what?
articles.text:
2028 referendum supporters say they have enough signatures to suspend new Mass. abortion law. Now what? | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Gov. Maura Healey reaches for a pen to sign an abortion law in August at the State House. (Ella Adams / SHNS)
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's daily morning newsletter, WBUR Today. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here.
Happy Halloween Eve! (All Hallows Eve-eve?) The National Weather Service says the trick-or-treating forecast " looks like a treat," and Salem is expecting even bigger crowds than usual for its 400th anniversary. Here's a guide for visitors.
(Reminder: today is also the last day of in-person early voting for the midterms in Massachusetts, in case you want to get ahead of the Tuesday rush.)
Now, to the news:
One ballot battle after another: Supporters of a petition to hold a 2028 referendum on Massachusetts' new abortion law say they've collected nearly double the signatures necessary to suspend the law. The "Compassionate Care Coalition" announced yesterday that they collected 97,276 signatures from Massachusetts voters in support of their effort. They need to file at least 37,289 by next Friday to put the referendum on the 2028 ballot — and at least 49,716 to suspend the law until that election. "We are grateful to every volunteer, pastor and parish staffer who carried a clipboard," coalition chair Sam Miele said in a statement. "Because of them, voters will have the final say."
Catch up: The law — which is set to take effect next Sunday, Nov. 8. — gets rid of restrictions on abortions for pregnancies beyond 24 weeks, putting the decision up to "the professional judgment" of the doctor. Gov. Maura Healey signed it in August, saying the measure gets the government out of "incredibly rare," painful choices for patients. Antiabortion activists and Catholic Church leaders backed the repeal effort last month, deriding the abortion law as one of the most permissive in the country.
What's next: The final tally of signatures still needs to be certified by Secretary of State Bill Galvin's office. Galvin spokesperson Debra O'Malley said yesterday that they had "received a small quantity of petitions," but expect more to be filed before the Nov. 6 deadline. O'Malley said it typically takes one to two weeks to review and certify the signatures, a process that doesn't start until after all of them have been filed.
FYI: The potential suspension of the law only takes effect after Galvin's office has certified the signature total. Healey also has the ability to block — or even undo — the suspension by attaching an emergency preamble to the law ( like she did with the 2024 gun law) anytime up until the 2028 election. In a statement Thursday, Healey spokesperson Jacqueline Manning said the governor "continues to monitor the referendum process and evaluate options." "This law is for parents facing some of the most painful and devastating circumstances imaginable and making sure these decisions are made between a woman and her doctor," Manning said.
Meanwhile on Beacon Hill: Consider Healey's proposal to suspend the state's gas tax all but officially dead. The Massachusetts Senate — whose leaders had actually expressed an inkling of openness to the idea — released its closeout budget bill Thursday. And while the $2.6 billion spending bill includes a number of policy add-ons, a gas tax suspension is not one of them. It comes after the House left out the proposal from its version of the bill last week.
What is in it? Like the House, the Senate proposal dedicates $1.8 billion for MassHealth and includes money to hire 200 new caseworkers at the agency that handles food stamps and other benefits. State House News Service has more here on the other policy proposals the Senate added to the bill.
A graphic showing the partial Green Line closure this weekend. (MBTA)
Green Line ghosting: The MBTA is giving riders more tricks than treats this weekend. The Green Line's downtown tunnel between North Station and Kenmore will be closed Saturday and Sunday due to signal upgrades — as will part of the B branch and the southern E branch. Click here for more on shuttle buses and other free public transit alternatives.
Plan ahead: An even bigger, nine-day partial Green Line closure (affecting the C branch, too) starts next weekend. Get the details on that here.
Meanwhile: The T announced this morning that Red Line trains can officially go up to 50 mph between North Quincy to JFK/UMass, as the agency promised last week.
He's back: After a record four sold-out shows at Fenway Park this summer, Noah Kahan is running it back. The Vermont native announced a 2027 stadium tour yesterday that includes four more concerts at Fenway (rather than Gillette Stadium; make of that what you will). Those shows take place May 29 to June 2 — with tickets going on sale in November.
Save the date: Boston Mayor Michelle Wu announced that this year's final Open Newbury — a special "holiday stroll" edition — will be Dec. 6.
P.S.— Which two Massachusetts cities will get federal poll monitors on Election Day? Take our Boston News Quiz and see how well you know the stories we covered this week compared to other WBUR readers.

articles.title: Jurors listen as prosecutor, Farwell attorney tell very different stories about Birchmore's death
articles.text:
Jurors listen as prosecutor, Farwell attorney tell very different stories about Birchmore's death | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
A federal prosecutor on Friday delivered their closing statement in the case against Matthew Farwell, telling jurors he killed Sandra Birchmore to "end any possibility she would expose him." Farwell’s defense attorney, in turn, countered by raising doubts about the government's case.
"They cannot reach the burden of proof," defense attorney Kimberly Stevens told jurors. “Why? Because Matthew didn't kill her."
Friday’s closing arguments capped five weeks of testimony in the high-profile case, which now heads to jury deliberations. Prosecutors argue Farwell, a former Stoughton police detective strangled and killed Sandra Birchmore in her Canton apartment and then staged the scene to look like a suicide by hanging.
Defense attorneys, meanwhile, have argued that Birchmore, who was pregnant, did take her own life because she was distraught Farwell ended their relationship.
The state’s medical examiner initially ruled Birchmore’s death a suicide, but revised her determination after federal authorities got involved in the case.
Much of the trial focused on dueling expert testimony about Birchmore’s injuries, including a break in a small U-shaped neck bone, which prosecutors say shows she died by strangulation not suicide.
Another key issue during the trial was Birchmore’s mental health, with Farwell’s defense team arguing that Birchmore struggled emotionally and a history of self-harm.
Farwell, 41, faces two federal charges: killing a witness or victim and causing the death of an unborn child. If convicted, he could spend the rest of his life in prison.
In the government's closing argument, prosecutor Brian Fogerty told jurors that Matthew Farwell didn't go to Sandra Birchmore's apartment on Feb. 1, 2021 to end their relationship.
"He went to clean up the mess that he created for himself years earlier — a mess that could bring serious charges and destroy his life," Fogerty told jurors. "He cleaned up the mess by taking Sandra’s life.”
Prosecutors allege Farwell killed Birchmore to keep her from telling authorities Farwell had sexually abused her when she was 15 years old. They met when she was a member of Stoughton Police Department’s youth explorers program where Farwell volunteered as an instructor.
Birchmore was eight to 10 weeks pregnant at the time of her death and believed the child was Farwell’s. DNA testing conducted years later would find another man was the biological father of the fetus.
Throughout the trial, prosecutors relied on a trove of 40,000 text messages, largely between Farwell and Birchmore, who met when she joined the police youth program at 13 years old. Prosecutors say the texts show Farwell had sex with Birchmore when she was a minor. The two continued a long-running affair that involved Farwell, a married police detective, texting Birchmore about violent sexual fantasies involving choking.
In the months before her death, according to text messages, Birchmore pressed Farwell to get her pregnant and threatened to tell his wife about the affair. After getting pregnant in late 2020, Birchmore told Farwell that he was the father and wanted him to sign the birth certificate. According to one of Birchmore’s friends, Farwell responded angrily and pushed her to the ground during a fight.
A turning point, according to prosecutors, happened on Jan. 20, 2021. That’s when someone called the Stoughton Police Department and disclosed the relationship between Birchmore and Farwell to a police dispatcher. Prosecutors allege after the call, which Farwell told the dispatcher to never discuss again according to testimony, he decided to kill Birchmore to prevent her from exposing their relationship.
“The defendant knew that Sandra wouldn’t stay quiet,” Forgety told jurors Friday. “She was telling people about their relationship and the information actually got to the Stoughton Police Department. And he knew that.”
Twelve days later, on Feb. 1, 2021, prosecutors allege Farwell strangled Birchmore in her Canton apartment. Police later found Birchmore’s body on the floor of her bedroom with a duffel bag strap around her neck. The strap was tied to the doorknob of her closet.
Testifying for the government, Dr. William Smock, a forensic medical expert, reviewed Birchmore’s autopsy and found she died by “homicidal strangulation” and that her death scene was staged to look like a suicide. Smock said Birchmore’s hyoid bone in her neck had fractured inward, which he said happens during strangulation.
Referencing Smock’s testimony, Fogerty told jurors that none of the medical experts hired by the defense could point to a single instance “where a young person like Sandra … had suffered a fracture from a seated hanging position like the one she was found in.”
In her closing for Farwell’s defense, Kimberly Stevens challenged the government’s conclusions and reminded jurors that the government must prove Farwell’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
Similar to the prosecution, Farwell’s defense team relied heavily on the voluminous text history between Birchmore and Farwell. On Friday, Stevens highlighted messages that – along with Birchmore’s journal entries and web searches – purport to show a young woman who had mental health struggles and a history of self-harm.
One of those searches was for the color of a suicide ribbon.
“What better insight into a person’s mind and thinking that they would search for such a thing?” said Stevens.
Stevens said Birchmore killed herself after Farwell went to her apartment on Feb 1. 2021 and told her that he wasn’t the father of her baby and that their relationship was over.
Stevens told jurors to “examine what was in Miss Birchmore’s head and in heart and in her life at the moment that Matt broke up with her and return a verdict of not guilty because he is not guilty.”

articles.title: Women who fought back take center stage in ‘The Wash,’ ‘1972’ and ‘The Getaway Driver’
articles.text:
Women who fought back take center stage in ‘The Wash,’ ‘1972’ and ‘The Getaway Driver’ | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Members of the company in performance for A.R.T.’s world premiere production of "1972." (Courtesy A.R.T./Nile Scott Studios)
One step toward justice can launch a revolution.
Three productions now onstage — " The Wash,” “ The Getaway Driver” and “ 1972” — center on the collective power of women willing to fight for what they believe in.
In Front Porch Arts Collective’s beautiful production of Kelundra Smith’s “The Wash,” Black laundresses in Atlanta are tired of being paid in rice and beans, or not at all, for their backbreaking work. To fix it, they knock on customers’ doors to collect what they’re owed. But after many slammed doors and threats of violence, and with back taxes owed on the house they work from, the women change tactics.
The story is inspired by the Black washerwomen who in 1881 organized the Atlanta Washerwomen Society and went on strike to set fair wages and reform labor practices. Smith, a journalist and playwright, first learned of  the story at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture and was so struck by it that she decided to write a play.
Though the women in Smith’s script are fictional, the impact they represent is very real. Smith’s writing sings under Tasia A. Jones’ excellent direction, supported by Lindsey McWhorter’s artful choreography, Janie E. Howland’s scenic design and Pamela Hersch’s projections of swaying trees, stained glass and more. The mesmerizing cast includes MaConnia Chesser as Jeanie, MarHadoo Effeh as Thomasine, Eliza Fichter as Mozelle, McWhorter as Anna, Jada Saintlouis as Charity and Kiera Prusmack as Jewel. McWhorter’s Anna leads the charge as the strike’s chief organizer, and Chesser is in rare form as Jeanie, Anna’s best friend and chief skeptic. Chesser’s antics kept the crowd laughing throughout, and McWhorter was moving as Anna explaining that the group’s work isn’t just for them, but for everyone.
Cast members of the Front Porch Art Collective’s "The Wash," Marhadoo Effeh, Lindsey McWhorter, MaConnia Chesser, Jada Saintlouis and Kiera Prusmack. (Courtesy Front Porch Art Collective/Ken Yotsukura)
As the women — who mobilized thousands of strikers, including some white women — grow more powerful and successful in their fight, costume designer Marissa Wolf moves their clothing from more muted tones to full skirts in primary colors, and finally, bold African-print robes, jackets and skirts. The deliberate shift seems to nod to the enslaved African ancestors who toiled without pay long before these women, letting them know that this fight was for them too.
A battle for the power to choose anchors the American Repertory Theater’s spellbinding production of “1972,” a world-premiere musical with music and lyrics by Chadwick Stokes, of the Boston-based indie bands Dispatch and State Radio. Stokes wrote the book with Jessie Nelson, who also directs. In the show, Hannah (a stellar Gracie McGraw), 19 and pregnant, hops a train to escape an abusive relationship. Along the way, she makes friends and tries to decide what to do about the baby. But in 1972 abortion was illegal in most of the U.S. and an illegal procedure could land a woman in jail — or kill her.  Hannah meets Louisa (a magnificent Jackera Davis), a preacher’s daughter who went through a harrowing experience trying to get an abortion.
The music in the show is excellent, and the songs (even the turn-off your cell phone song at the show’s start) are sung and played by about a dozen talented musicians and singers. There are drums,  bass, harmonica, trumpet, the violin and more that help set the vibe and move the show along that’s set in a red-painted train caboose in front of gorgeous projections.  Every single cast member sings throughout the show that introduces us to Hannah’s plight and the Janes, an organization of women who help women have safe abortions. Head Jane Harlan (a superb Khaila Wilcoxon), sings about their work, while introducing all of the other Jane heroines as they band together to help Hannah who is client 10,363.
The real-life Jane Collective reportedly performed 11,000 abortions between 1969 and 1973, when the Supreme Court’s Roe v. Wade decision legalized abortion nationwide.
Rebecca Gibel and Rachael Warren in "The Getaway Driver" at Central Square Theater. (Courtesy Central Square Theater/Nile Scott Studios)
In “The Getaway Driver,” protesting the Vietnam War lands Katherine Ann Power in a world of trouble. Central Square Theater’s production of the play by Deborah Salem Smith and Charlie Thurston mostly details the life of Power (Rebecca Gibel) and is based on the true story of Power and Clare Schroeder. A college-educated student from a stable home, Power joins a group of other passionate young people who opposed the Vietnam war. But after a bank robbery ends in the death of a police officer, the perpetrators’ worlds fall apart.  Told largely through monologues by Gibel and Rachael Warren, who plays Clare, the daughter of the slain officer, the show features a set by An-Lin Dauber (who is also the costume designer) and video design by Peter Sasha Hurowitz. Much of the play traces Power’s downward spiral and Clare’s grief and desire for revenge. Though the premise for the show is an intriguing one, the emotional high stakes didn’t capture me until a tearful scene in which Power — who spent 23 years on the run, the longest of any woman in FBI most wanted history — stands before the parole board explaining herself. It made me pause to consider how quickly a life can turn upside down, and how hard it is to atone for it.
The Front Porch Art Collective’s production of “ The Wash,” runs through Nov. 22 at Stanford Calderwood Pavilion at the BCA in the Roberts Studio Theatre. The American Repertory Theater’s “ 1972” runs through Dec. 6 at Farkas Hall in Harvard Square and Central Square Theater’s “ The Get

articles.title: 7 holiday markets to visit in Boston and beyond
articles.text:
7 holiday markets to visit in Boston and beyond | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Light displays at Snowport. (Lindsay Ahern/Boston Seaport by WS)
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's Saturday morning newsletter, The Weekender. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox,  sign up here.
Don’t let this week's warm weather distract you: The holiday shopping season is nearly here, and markets with their jingling bells, cheesy sandwiches and cups of cocoa will be popping up over the next few weeks.
But we know heading into the city to wait in a long line isn’t everyone’s ideal experience. So this year, in addition to some local favorites, we’re suggesting a few markets all around eastern Massachusetts.
Snowport
100 Seaport Blvd., Boston
(Nov. 6 – Dec. 27)
Boston’s largest holiday market made its annual return on Friday, with over 125 vendors selling candles, jewelry, clothing, novelty gifts, art prints and more. Open seven days a week, they’ve got food, themed bars, iceless curling, Christmas trees for sale, and the market's mascot, Betty the Yeti, roaming around. (For a new diversion, head over two blocks to Ballers, a padel and pickleball club that unveiled a winter takeover Friday where you can skate on a synthetic ice rink and sip hot chocolate.)
Admission: Entry to Snowport is free. But if you’d like to skip the line, fast-pass tickets are $15 for adults and $7 for veterans and children aged 6 to 17. Skating at Ballers Boston, which includes skate rentals, is $20 per hour for adults and $15 per hour for kids under 12.
Aerial view of Snowport's themed bars. (Courtesy Boston Seaport by WS)
SoWa Christmas Market
550 Harrison Ave., Boston
(Nov. 20 - Dec. 27)
The holiday market at the SoWa Power Station is back this year with more than 100 vendors and a slew of new events and activities. You can get pictures with Santa, meet the Grinch, get a caricature done on opening day or build your own holiday bouquet on Dec. 15 (be sure to register in advance). They’ve also got a full entertainment calendar with live music and line dancing nights.
Admission: Tickets are $10. Children 12 and under can get in free.
Paradise City Arts Festival
181 Royal Plaza Dr. West, Marlborough
(Nov. 20-22)
This one’s for the MetroWest folks. The Paradise City Arts Festival is coming to Marlborough’s Royal Plaza Trade Center the weekend before Thanksgiving. This creative showcase features over 175 artists selling their handmade goods, from paintings and photography to wood furniture to stuffed animals. Organizers recommend allotting three to four hours to peruse all the galleries while the market is open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Friday and Saturday and 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Sunday.
Admission: Single day tickets online are $16 or $24 for all three days of the festival. Students can get in for $10 if they present an ID at the box office. Children under 15 get in free.
Boston Women's Market
Multiple locations in Somerville
(Nov. 22 and Nov. 29)
The Boston Women’s Market will be held twice this month at two different locations in Somerville. The first is at Warehouse XI in Union Square from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Nov. 22, and the second is at Arts at the Armory from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Nov. 29. Both markets will feature more than 30 local, women-owned businesses. But it’s only at the Warehouse XI installment that you’ll be able to enter the market’s golden ticket hunt. There will be five tickets hidden throughout the venue — and if you find one, you’ll win a $50 gift card to spend with any of the vendors at the market that day.
Admission: Free to attend.
Trustees Holiday Market at Castle Hill
290 Argilla Rd., Ipswich
(Dec. 3)
Up on the North Shore, The Trustees of Reservations are inviting the public to a holiday market at Castle Hill on the Crane Estate. Seven different businesses and institutions on properties owned by the Trustees — including Appleton Farms, the deCordova Museum and the Fruitlands Museum — will be selling small gifts and artisanal foods at the market, which runs from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. You’ll also be able to see the first floor of Castle Hill’s Great House decked out in all its holiday splendor, so if you’ve never visited this historic property, this is your chance.
Admission: Free to attend.
Plymouth Holiday Market
83 Court St., Plymouth
(Dec. 3)
Down on the South Shore, Plymouth is hosting a holiday market with more than 90 vendors at Plymouth Memorial Hall. Expect to find jewelry, home decor, giftable art and specialty foods from local makers and food trucks outside of the venue from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Admission: Tickets are $6 at the door. Children under 12 can get in free.
Harvard Square Holiday Fair
57 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge
(Dec. 11-13, Dec. 18-20)
The Harvard Square Holiday Fair will take place in the lower level of the Galeria building (on the corner of JFK and Winthrop streets) during two weekends in December. The annual artisan market encourages visitors to chat with vendors and learn more about the treasures they’re picking up, from jewelry and pottery to carved wooden boxes and miniatures. You can drop by on Fridays between noon and 7 p.m., on Saturdays from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., and on Sundays from noon to 6 p.m.
Admission: Free to attend.
P.S. — Want more fun winter ideas? Look no further than our Field Guide to Boston in winter, with ways to get outside as the days grow darker and colder.

articles.title: Boston city councilor plans to seek legal action after T general manager fails to attend hearing
articles.text:
Boston city councilor plans to seek legal action after T general manager fails to attend hearing | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Miniard Culpepper speaks at the forum at the Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)
A Boston city councilor plans to pursue legal action against the leader of the MBTA for not appearing at a hearing, despite being issued a subpoena.
Last week, the City Council voted to subpoena T general manager and interim transportation secretary Phil Eng to testify about the  controversial Blue Hill Avenue redevelopment project. The hearing, co-sponsored by councilors Miniard Culpepper and Brian Worrell, was a follow up meeting to discuss civil rights and transportation equity — in addition to the possibility of bringing an Orange Line extension to Blue Hill Avenue.
A spokesperson for the MBTA told WBUR in an email that Eng would not be attending “due to a previously planned vacation with his family.”
Culpepper essentially canceled the meeting a half hour after it was scheduled to start Friday because of Eng’s absence.
“We had planned to put Mr. Eng under oath," Culpepper told WBUR after formally ending the hearing. "We had planned to have councilors make opening statements. We had planned to have the public here to testify. All of that was based on Philip Eng showing up to testify at this hearing.”
The MBTA said Eng is willing to participate in a community meeting on the hearing topics or meet directly with city councilors. Culpepper said he isn’t interested in meeting with Eng under those conditions.
“We’re not meeting with him in community meetings or in closed door rooms where he tells us things that they don't plan to commit to,” Culpepper said. “We need this to be in public.”
Culpepper said he intends to go to court to enforce the subpoena. He will need the City Council’s approval to do so.
“We're preparing to get ready to go to court, those are the next steps,” he said.
The MBTA has not yet responded to WBUR's request for comment on Culpepper’s plan to enforce the subpoena.
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said the T and Eng have a history of collaboration with the city, attending community meetings and participating in “briefings where elected officials have been able to ask questions."
“There was a scheduling conflict, and I do not believe that subpoenas are a productive way to engage with the partners who are working alongside us every day,” Wu told reporters at an unrelated press event Friday.
WBUR's Eve Zuckoff contributed to this report.
